Regions / Data Science

Data Science

In progress

Students ask questions, collect and clean data, look for patterns, build simple models, and communicate what the data shows.

Topics

  • Statistical questions
  • Collecting and cleaning data
  • Visualization
  • Models and prediction
  • Sampling and bias
Open the Data Science mapFind it on the map

Places and activity ideas

Each place on the Data Science map is one step of the journey, with an unplugged activity idea. Select a place to open it on the map.

  • AskAsking Questions

    Activity idea: Question Sort. Students sort question cards into statistical and non-statistical, then sharpen vague questions into ones data could answer.

  • SampleSampling

    Activity idea: Bean Bags. Students estimate the mix of colors in a bag of beans from small samples, then see how a biased scoop gives the wrong answer.

  • CollectData Collection

    Activity idea: Data Cards. The class designs a short survey, fills out one data card each, and discusses what the cards leave out.

  • QuestionOutliers

    Activity idea: The Odd Card. A planted outlier in the deck: groups decide whether it is a typo to fix or a real case to explain.

  • CleanData Cleaning

    Activity idea: Messy Deck. Groups clean a printed deck with typos, blanks, and duplicates, and record each fix they made.

  • OrganizeOrganizing Data

    Activity idea: Paper Table. Students lay the cards out as rows and columns on the floor and decide each column's data type.

  • ExploreExploring Data

    Activity idea: Sort and Count. Groups sort and tally the deck to find patterns, clusters, and relationships.

  • VisualizeVisualization

    Activity idea: Human Charts. Students stand to form a bar chart or scatterplot on floor axes, then redraw it by hand; a gallery walk of misleading charts follows.

  • ModelModeling

    Activity idea: Decision Tree. Groups build a paper decision tree that sorts the cards, then test it on cards it has not seen.

  • PredictPrediction

    Activity idea: Forecast Cards. Students make predictions from their model with a confidence level, then check them against held-back cards.

  • InterpretInterpreting Results

    Activity idea: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning. Groups write a claim on poster paper with the evidence from their cards, and classmates challenge it.

  • ReflectPrivacy and Fairness

    Activity idea: What the Cards Reveal. Students work out what can be guessed about a person from a few "harmless" fields, and who their model treats unfairly.

Big ideas

  1. Data is made by people for a purpose. Every dataset reflects choices about what to collect, how, and from whom.
  2. Data must be organized and cleaned. Structure (rows, columns, types) and cleaning come before analysis.
  3. Visualizations tell stories, and can mislead. Choosing and reading charts critically.
  4. Patterns and models help us predict, with uncertainty. From trends to simple models to the ideas behind machine learning.
  5. Data has consequences. Privacy, bias, and fairness in how data is collected and used.

These follow the data investigation cycle: ask a question → collect or consider data → analyze → interpret and communicate.

Learning progression

Middle school (6–8)High school (9–12)
QuestionsAsk statistical questions about familiar topicsForm questions about complex systems
Collect and cleanCollect class data on paper data cards; spot and fix messy entriesSort, filter, and reshape a large printed deck of data cards
VisualizeDraw a fitting chart by hand; read charts criticallyBuild human and hand-drawn charts; find and fix misleading ones
ModelDescribe trends and make predictionsBuild and test models by hand, such as a decision tree from data cards
ImpactsPersonal data and privacyBias, fairness, and data in decision-making

Standards

CSTA K–12 Computer Science Standards, Data and Analysis: 2-DA-07 to 2-DA-09 (grades 6–8), 3A-DA-09 to 3A-DA-12 (grades 9–10), and 3B-DA-05 to 3B-DA-07 (grades 11–12).

Activities

Full activities for this region are being written. Each will be unplugged, with a teacher guide and print-ready handouts, and students will need no technology.
